claims.text: As-solid-solution high-entropy alloys have severe lattice distortions.
As-solid-solution high-entropy alloys have complex local chemical ordering.
The impediment of dislocation mobility by lattice distortion occurs under high-strain-rate deformation.
Restricted dislocation mobility promotes deformation twinning or stress-induced phase transformation.
The promoted alternative deformation mechanisms enhance strain hardening.
Twinning or transformation-induced plasticity allows high strength and ductility to be sustained simultaneously during dynamic loading.
A controlled thermal treatment can partially relax lattice distortions while preserving the overall phase composition.
Relaxing lattice distortions reduces the activation or effectiveness of twinning or transformation-induced plasticity under dynamic loading.
The as-solid-solution alloy will have higher dynamic yield strength than the thermally treated control.
The as-solid-solution alloy will retain greater ductility than the thermally treated control at high strain rates.
The as-solid-solution and thermally treated samples will exhibit different dislocation structures.
The as-solid-solution and thermally treated samples will exhibit different amounts or morphologies of deformation twins.
The proposed mechanism should operate under high-strain-rate loading from approximately 25°C to 700°C.
The proposed mechanism may cease to dominate under quasi-static loading or at extreme temperatures.
Constituent-atom lattice-parameter differences create friction that hinders partial-dislocation motion and produces hardening.
Minor compositional variations or secondary-phase precipitation may affect strength, ductility, and deformation behavior.
